Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

> George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Selection process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selection process")]

Honoree recommendations are accepted from the general public,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and the Kennedy Center initiated a Special Honors Advisory Committee, which comprises members of the board of trustees as well as past honorees and distinguished artists.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The executive committee of the board of trustees selects the honoree recipients based on their impact and contributions to American culture and excellence in music, dance, theater, opera, motion pictures or television.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The selections are typically announced sometime between July and September. Most honorees are [Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans"), with non-U.S. citizen honorees typically hailing from elsewhere in the [anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere").

## Events

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Events")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg/250px-Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kennedy_Center_(46399777861).jpg)

The Kennedy Center lights up in rainbow colors every year in the weeks preceding the ceremony.

The invitation-only, weekend-long ceremony includes the Chairman's Luncheon, the State Department dinner, White House reception, and the Honors gala performances and supper.

The Chairman's Luncheon is held on Saturday at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"). Surrounded by the honorees, the chairman of the board of trustees launches the event with a welcoming speech. At that evening's reception and dinner at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), presided over by the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), the honorees are introduced and the Honors medallions are presented by the chairman of the board.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The wide rainbow-colored ribbon then hung around the necks of the recipients and prominently noticeable when the events are televised, symbolizes "a spectrum of many skills within the performing arts" according to creator [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

On Sunday, there is an early-evening [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") reception,[[22]](#cite_note-22) traditionally hosted by the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States"), followed by the Honors gala performance at the Kennedy Center and supper.

Prior to 2017, there had been three occasions in which the president did not attend the gala performance. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") did not attend in 1979 during the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"); First Lady [Rosalynn Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Carter "Rosalynn Carter") served as his surrogate.[[23]](#cite_note-23) President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") was on a trip to [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") and could not attend in 1989; First Lady [Barbara Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bush "Barbara Bush") served as his surrogate.[[24]](#cite_note-24) President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") was on a trip to [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") and could not attend in 1994; First Lady [Hillary Rodham Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Rodham_Clinton "Hillary Rodham Clinton") served as his surrogate.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

For the 2015 gala performance, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") joined First Lady [Michelle Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Obama "Michelle Obama") late after addressing the nation in a live telecast from the White House.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In 2017, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and First Lady [Melania Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melania_Trump "Melania Trump") decided not to participate in events honoring recipients of the 2017 Kennedy Center Honor [Jump to content](#bodyContent)

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

> George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

> George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Selection process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selection process")]

Honoree recommendations are accepted from the general public,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and the Kennedy Center initiated a Special Honors Advisory Committee, which comprises members of the board of trustees as well as past honorees and distinguished artists.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The executive committee of the board of trustees selects the honoree recipients based on their impact and contributions to American culture and excellence in music, dance, theater, opera, motion pictures or television.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The selections are typically announced sometime between July and September. Most honorees are [Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans"), with non-U.S. citizen honorees typically hailing from elsewhere in the [anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere").

## Events

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Events")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg/250px-Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kennedy_Center_(46399777861).jpg)

The Kennedy Center lights up in rainbow colors every year in the weeks preceding the ceremony.

The invitation-only, weekend-long ceremony includes the Chairman's Luncheon, the State Department dinner, White House reception, and the Honors gala performances and supper.

The Chairman's Luncheon is held on Saturday at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"). Surrounded by the honorees, the chairman of the board of trustees launches the event with a welcoming speech. At that evening's reception and dinner at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), presided over by the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), the honorees are introduced and the Honors medallions are presented by the chairman of the board.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The wide rainbow-colored ribbon then hung around the necks of the recipients and prominently noticeable when the events are televised, symbolizes "a spectrum of many skills within the performing arts" according to creator [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

On Sunday, there is an early-evening [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") reception,[[22]](#cite_note-22) traditionally hosted by the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States"), followed by the Honors gala performance at the Kennedy Center and supper.

Prior to 2017, there had been three occasions in which the president did not attend the gala performance. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") did not attend in 1979 during the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"); First Lady [Rosalynn Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Carter "Rosalynn Carter") served as his surrogate.[[23]](#cite_note-23) President [George H. Bush") was on a trip to [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") and could not attend in 1989; First Lady [Barbara Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bush "Barbara Bush") served as his surrogate.[[24]](#cite_note-24) President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") was on a trip to [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") and could not attend in 1994; First Lady [Hillary Rodham Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Rodham_Clinton "Hillary Rodham Clinton") served as his surrogate.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

For the 2015 gala performance, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") joined First Lady [Michelle Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Obama "Michelle Obama") late after addressing the nation in a live telecast from the White House.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

> George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Selection process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selection process")]

Honoree recommendations are accepted from the general public,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and the Kennedy Center initiated a Special Honors Advisory Committee, which comprises members of the board of trustees as well as past honorees and distinguished artists.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The executive committee of the board of trustees selects the honoree recipients based on their impact and contributions to American culture and excellence in music, dance, theater, opera, motion pictures or television.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The selections are typically announced sometime between July and September. Most honorees are [Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans"), with non-U.S. citizen honorees typically hailing from elsewhere in the [anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere").

## Events

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Events")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg/250px-Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kennedy_Center_(46399777861).jpg)

The Kennedy Center lights up in rainbow colors every year in the weeks preceding the ceremony.

The invitation-only, weekend-long ceremony includes the Chairman's Luncheon, the State Department dinner, White House reception, and the Honors gala performances and supper.

The Chairman's Luncheon is held on Saturday at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"). Surrounded by the honorees, the chairman of the board of trustees launches the event with a welcoming speech. At that evening's reception and dinner at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), presided over by the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), the honorees are introduced and the Honors medallions are presented by the chairman of the board.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The wide rainbow-colored ribbon then hung around the necks of the recipients and prominently noticeable when the events are televised, symbolizes "a spectrum of many skills within the performing arts" according to creator [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

On Sunday, there is an early-evening [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") reception,[[22]](#cite_note-22) traditionally hosted by the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States"), followed by the Honors gala performance at the Kennedy Center and supper.

Prior to 2017, there had been three occasions in which the president did not attend the gala performance. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") did not attend in 1979 during the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"); First Lady [Rosalynn Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Carter "Rosalynn Carter") served as his surrogate.[[23]](#cite_note-23) President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") was on a trip to [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") and could not attend in 1989; First Lady [Barbara Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bush "Barbara Bush") served as his surrogate.[[24]](#cite_note-24) President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") was on a trip to [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") and could not attend in 1994; First Lady [Hillary Rodham Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Rodham_Clinton "Hillary Rodham Clinton") served as his surrogate.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

For the 2015 gala performance, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") joined First Lady [Michelle Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Obama "Michelle Obama") late after addressing the nation in a live telecast from the White House.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In 2017, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and First Lady [Melania Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melania_Trump "Melania Trump") decided not to participate in events honoring recipients of the 2017 Kennedy Center Honor

**Rosa Ponzillo**, known as **Rosa Ponselle** (January 22, 1897 – May 25, 1981) was an American [operatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera") [dramatic soprano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_soprano "Dramatic soprano").

She sang mainly at the New York [Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera "Metropolitan Opera") and is generally considered to have been one of the greatest sopranos of the 20th century.[[1]](#cite_note-AH-1)

She was born Rosa Ponzillo on January 22, 1897, in [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"), the youngest of three children. The family lived on the city's west side in a neighbourhood chiefly populated by immigrants from [Southern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Italy "Southern Italy"), first at the corner of Lewis Avenue and Bartlett Street, then on Foster Street, where Ponselle was born, moving when she was three to Springdale Avenue. Her parents were Italian immigrants from [Caiazzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caiazzo "Caiazzo"), near [Caserta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caserta "Caserta"). Ponselle had an exceptionally mature voice at an early age and, at least in her early years, sang on natural endowment with little, if any, vocal training. Instead, her early prowess as a piano student (which was cultivated by a local music teacher, Anna Ryan, the organist of a nearby Catholic church), seemed to incline Rosa to instrumental rather than vocal music. But with the influence and example of her older sister, Carmela, who was then pursuing a career as a cabaret singer, Rosa began to augment her engagements as a silent-movie accompanist in and around Meriden by singing popular ballads to her audiences while the projectionist changed film reels. By 1914, her reputation as a singer led to a long-term engagement at the San Carlino theater, one of the largest movie houses in [New Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Haven,_Connecticut "New Haven, Connecticut"), near the [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") campus.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## Vaudeville

By then, Carmela was already an established singer in [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") after her debut in *The Girl from Brighton*, a 1912 [Broadway musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre"). Three years later, in 1915, Carmela brought Rosa to audition for her vaudeville agent. In spite of being markedly overweight (a stark contrast to the fashion-model physique of her older sister), Rosa impressed with her voice, and she was hired to perform with Carmela as a "sister act". Between 1915 and 1918, the Ponzillo Sisters (also known as "Those Tailored Italian Girls") became a headlining act on the [Keith Vaudeville Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Vaudeville_Circuit "Keith Vaudeville Circuit"), appearing in all the major Keith theaters and earning a substantial income in the process. The sisters' act consisted of traditional ballads, popular Italian songs, and operatic arias and duets.

In 1918, after Carmela and Rosa demanded a substantial fee increase from the [Keith Vaudeville Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Vaudeville_Circuit "Keith Vaudeville Circuit"), their act was dropped. At the time, Carmela was studying in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") with a well-connected voice teacher/agent named William Thorner. Thorner auditioned Rosa, and agreed to give her lessons. (Rosa later denied that Thorner had ever given her voice lessons, but her statements on the subject are contradictory.) Although initially less impressed with Rosa's future prospects than with Carmela's, Thorner changed his opinion after the legendary baritone [Victor Maurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Maurel "Victor Maurel"), whom [Giuseppe Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi") had chosen to create [Iago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iago "Iago") in *[Otello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otello "Otello")*, auditioned both sisters at his friend Thorner's request. Soon afterward, Thorner persuaded the [Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera "Metropolitan Opera")'s great star [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor") [Enrico Caruso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Caruso "Enrico Caruso"), to visit his studio and hear Carmela and Rosa sing. Caruso was usually wary when asked to listen to amateur singers, but he was deeply impressed with Rosa's voice. Caruso arranged an audition for Rosa attended by the Met's general manager, [Giulio Gatti-Casazza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Gatti-Casazza "Giulio Gatti-Casazza"). Gatti was equally impressed with Rosa's singing and offered her a contract for the Met's 1918/1919 season.

## Metropolitan Opera debut and early operatic career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rosa_Ponselle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Metropolitan Opera debut and early operatic career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Ponselle_Caruso_Forza_del_Destino_-_black_%26_white.jpg/250px-Ponselle_Caruso_Forza_del_Destino_-_black_%26_white.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ponselle_Caruso_Forza_del_Destino_-_black_&_white.jpg)

José Mardones, Enrico Caruso and Rosa Ponselle in *La forza del destino* at the Metropolitan Opera, 1918

Rosa Ponselle made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera on November 15, 1918, just a few days after [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") had ended, as Leonora in [Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi")'s *[La forza del destino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_forza_del_destino "La forza del destino")*, opposite Caruso and [Giuseppe De Luca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_De_Luca "Giuseppe De Luca"). It was her first performance on any opera stage. She was quite intimidated for being in the presence of Caruso, and in spite of an almost paralyzing case of nervousness (which she suffered from throughout her operatic career), she scored a tremendous success, both with the public and with the critics. *[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Times "New York Times")* critic [James Huneker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Huneker "James Huneker") wrote: "...what a promising debut! Added to her personal attractiveness, she possesses a voice of natural beauty that may prove a gold mine; it is vocal gold, anyhow, with its luscious lower and middle tones, dark, rich and ductile, brilliant in the upper register."[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In addition to Leonora, Ponselle's roles in the 1918/19 season included Santuzza in *[Cavalleria rusticana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalleria_rusticana "Cavalleria rusticana")*, Reiza in [Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Maria_von_Weber "Carl Maria von Weber")'s *[Oberon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberon_(Weber) "Oberon (Weber)")*, and Carmelita in the (unsuccessful) world premiere of [Joseph Carl Breil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Carl_Breil "Joseph Carl Breil")'s *[The Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_(opera) "The Legend (opera)")*.

In the following Met seasons, Ponselle's roles included the lead soprano roles in *[La Juive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Juive "La Juive")* (opposite Caruso's Eléazar, his final new role before his death in 1921), *[William Tell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tell_(opera) "William Tell (opera)")*, *[Ernani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernani "Ernani")*, *[Il trovatore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_trovatore "Il trovatore")*, *[Aida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aida "Aida")*, *[La Gioconda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Gioconda_(opera) "La Gioconda (opera)")*, *[Don Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Carlos "Don Carlos")*, *[L'Africaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Africaine "L'Africaine")*, *[L'amore dei tre re](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'amore_dei_tre_re "L'amore dei tre re")*, *[Andrea Chénier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Chénier "Andrea Chénier")*, *[La vestale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_vestale_(Spontini) "La vestale (Spontini)")*, and the role that many considered her greatest achievement, [Bellini's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincenzo_Bellini "Vincenzo Bellini") *[Norma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_(opera) "Norma (opera)")*, in the Met's historic 1927 revival. In addition to her operatic activities, which were centered at the Met, Ponselle had a lucrative concert career. A tour of the [West Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States "West Coast of the United States") included an appearance at the [Lobero Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobero_Theatre "Lobero Theatre") in Santa Barbara on March 14, 1927, in the Artist Series of the Community Arts Association's Music Branch, accompanied by pianist Stuart Ross. As her career progressed, Ponselle negotiated through her manager more concerts and exponentially higher fees before and after each Metropolitan Opera season.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

**Aleksandra Dionisyevna Danilova** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Александра Дионисьевна Данилова; November 20, 1903 – July 13, 1997) was a Russian-born [prima ballerina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prima_ballerina "Prima ballerina"), who became an American citizen. In 1989, she was recognized for lifetime achievements in ballet as a [Kennedy Center Honoree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexandra_Danilova&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Peterhof, Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petergof "Petergof") on November 20, 1903, she trained at the [Russian Imperial Ballet School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Imperial_Ballet_School "Russian Imperial Ballet School") in Leningrad (now [St. Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg "St. Petersburg")).[[5]](#cite_note-ind-5) She was one of the few Russian-trained ballerinas to tour outside Russia. Her first professional post was as a member of St. Petersburg's [Imperial Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Ballet "Imperial Ballet").

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexandra_Danilova&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

On July 4, 1924, Danilova in a group of four dancers led by [George Balanchine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Balanchine "George Balanchine") left Russia. They wanted to experience European art. Overwhelmed by Berlin of early Weimar culture, they then as Soviet ballet stars left on "a tour of Rhineland spa towns". In October these same four "principle dancers of the Russian National Ballet" were in London at The [Empire theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_Leicester_Square "Empire Leicester Square").[[6]](#cite_note-6) Discoverd by [Sergei Diaghilev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Diaghilev "Sergei Diaghilev") he auditioned them in Paris for his [Ballets Russes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballets_Russes "Ballets Russes"), Danilova as a dancer, Balanchine as a [choreographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choreographer "Choreographer").[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Danilova toured in Diaghilev's company. She and Balanchine lived together until the early 1930s. Diaghilev promoted her *ballerina*. After his death in 1929 she continued dancing, with [Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_Russe_de_Monte_Carlo "Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo"). As a leading performer of the company she often partnered with [Leonid Massine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Massine "Leonid Massine"), who served as its choreographer. Often the company toured in the United States and in Latin America. In the 1950s she famously partnered with [Frederic Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Franklin "Frederic Franklin"). Known in the dance world for her stellar qualities, and generally for her celebrity glamour and beautiful legs, Danilova was a ballet professional. She was long adored by her audience.[[1]](#cite_note-nyt-obit-1)

The Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo presented *[Gaîté Parisienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaîté_Parisienne "Gaîté Parisienne")* in the U.S. for the first time at the [Metropolitan Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera_House_(Lincoln_Center) "Metropolitan Opera House (Lincoln Center)"), New York, on 12 October 1938, with Danilova as the Glove Seller.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Portraying her as a vivacious, glamorous, sophisticated woman of the world,[[10]](#cite_note-10) Danilova in *Gaîté* became one of the attractions of the Ballet Russe, and the ballet often concluded a season's opening-night performance. On the opening night of the company's 1941 season in New York, when Danilova made her first entrance she was given a spontaneous ovation that stopped the show. Such show-stopping ovations thenceforth became a tradition of every opening-night *Gaîté* with Danilova.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Alexandra_Danilova_red_swan_tutu_02_%28NYPL%29.jpg/250px-Alexandra_Danilova_red_swan_tutu_02_%28NYPL%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexandra_Danilova_red_swan_tutu_02_(NYPL).jpg)

Danilova's "red swan" tutu, used when she danced the role of Odile in *[Swan Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swan_Lake "Swan Lake")* ([New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library"))

Danilova made her [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") debut in 1944's *[Song of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Norway "Song of Norway")*;[[1]](#cite_note-nyt-obit-1) her last ballet performance was in 1957. She made her [musical comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_comedy "Musical comedy") debut in 1958 in *[Oh, Captain!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh,_Captain! "Oh, Captain!")*. She appeared in a single scene, a dance with the show's star, [Tony Randall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Randall "Tony Randall"). (A year later, they performed it on an episode of *[The Dinah Shore Chevy Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dinah_Shore_Chevy_Show "The Dinah Shore Chevy Show")*, thus preserving it for posterity.) Unfortunately, *Oh, Captain!* was not a commercial success and closed a few months later. She was in financial straits when she came across Balanchine on the street in 1964. When he heard of her plight he instantly hired her to teach at the [School of American Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_American_Ballet "School of American Ballet"). In 1965, she sought and received approval from Balanchine to produce a spring workshop performance for the students. These workshops became an important preview for many outstanding dancers. Danilova remained there until her retirement in 1989.[[3]](#cite_note-nyt-ret-3)

In 1972, she staged a [New York City Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Ballet "New York City Ballet") production of the romantic ballet *[Les Syphides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Syphides "Les Syphides")*, under the original title, *[Chopiniana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chopiniana "Chopiniana")*. Two years later, in 1974, Balanchine choreographed a version of [Coppélia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coppélia "Coppélia") for the [New York City Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Ballet "New York City Ballet"). He was assisted by Danilova, who had performed the title role many times during her dancing career.[[12]](#cite_note-macaulay-12) She staged the Petipa choreography for Act II.

Danilova had a small, but nostalgically delightful, role (especially for those who knew her earlier work) in the 1977 movie *[The Turning Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Turning_Point_(1977_film) "The Turning Point (1977 film)")* as a ballet coach for upcoming ballerinas.

In 1986 she published an autobiography called *Choura*, her own personal nickname. The book won the 1986 [de la Torre Bueno Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_la_Torre_Bueno_Prize "De la Torre Bueno Prize").[[13]](#cite_note-13)

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexandra_Danilova&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

She had a long intimate relationship with [Balanchine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Balanchine "George Balanchine") after his divorce from [Tamara Geva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamara_Geva "Tamara Geva"), from 1926 to 1933, but they never married. They continued their professional partnership long after their romance ended. Danilova, who became an American citizen in 1946, was twice married, to Giuseppe Massera in 1934[[14]](#cite_note-14) and to Casimir Kokitch in 1941.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

## Ephemera

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexandra_Danilova&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ephemera")]

In [Hugh Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Martin "Hugh Martin")'s *Look Ma, I'm Dancin'* of 1948, a disillusioned would-be dancer contrasts her skills with the talents of some of the leading ballerinas of the day, including Markova and Pavlova. The song includes the line "And as for Alexandra Danilova, I know I'll never make a schlemiel of 'er."

## Death

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alexandra_Danilova&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Death")]

Danilova died on July 13, 1997, in New York.[[5]](#cite_note-ind-5) She had a [Russian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox "Russian Orthodox") funeral service, and was interred at [Oakland Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland_Cemetery_(Sag_Harbor,_New_York) "Oakland Cemetery (Sag Harbor, New York)"), [Sag Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sag_Harbor "Sag Harbor"), [Suffolk County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffolk_County,_New_York "Suffolk County, New York") — the same cemetery where [George Balanchine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Balanchine "George Balanchine") is buried.

**Martha Graham** (May 11, 1894 – April 1, 1991)[[1]](#cite_note-1) was an American modern dancer, teacher and choreographer responsible for creating the [Graham technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique").[[2]](#cite_note-TIME-2)

Graham danced and taught for over seventy years. She was the first dancer to perform at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), travel abroad as a cultural ambassador, and receive the highest civilian award of the US: the [Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom"). In her lifetime she received honors including the [Key to the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") of Paris and Japan's Imperial [Order of the Precious Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Precious_Crown "Order of the Precious Crown").

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Graham was born in [Allegheny City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania"), later to become part of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania, in 1894. Her father, George Graham, was an "alienist", a practitioner of an early form of [psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry "Psychiatry").[[3]](#cite_note-3) The Grahams were [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterians "Presbyterians"). Her father was a third-generation American of Irish descent. Graham's mother, Jane Beers, was a second-generation American of Irish, Scots-Irish, and English ancestry, and who claimed to be a tenth-generation descendant[[4]](#cite_note-4) of [Myles Standish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Standish "Myles Standish").[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) While her parents provided a comfortable environment in her youth, it was not one that encouraged dancing.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199812-7)

The Graham family moved to [Santa Maria, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria,_California "Santa Maria, California"), when Martha was fourteen years old.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199820-8) In 1911, she attended the first dance performance of her life, watching [Ruth St. Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_St._Denis "Ruth St. Denis") perform at the [Mason Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Opera_House "Mason Opera House") in Los Angeles.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199821-9) In the mid-1910s, Martha Graham began her studies at the newly created [Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn_School_of_Dancing_and_Related_Arts "Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts"), founded by Ruth St. Denis and [Ted Shawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Shawn "Ted Shawn"),[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) at which she would stay until 1923. In 1922, Graham performed one of Shawn's Egyptian dances with [Lillian Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Powell "Lillian Powell") in a short silent film by [Hugo Riesenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Riesenfeld "Hugo Riesenfeld") that attempted to synchronize a dance routine on film with a live orchestra and an onscreen conductor.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Graham left the Denishawn establishment in 1923 in order to become a featured dancer in the [Greenwich Village Follies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village_Follies "Greenwich Village Follies") revue for two years.

In 1925, Graham was employed at the [Eastman School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastman_School_of_Music "Eastman School of Music") where [Rouben Mamoulian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouben_Mamoulian "Rouben Mamoulian") was head of the School of Drama. Among other performances, together Mamoulian and Graham produced a short [two-color film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_motion_picture_film "Color motion picture film") called *The Flute of Krishna,* featuring Eastman students. Mamoulian left Eastman shortly thereafter and Graham chose to leave also, even though she was asked to stay on.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1926, the [Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Center_of_Contemporary_Dance "Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance") was established, in a small studio on the [Upper East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_East_Side "Upper East Side") of New York City. On April 18 of the same year[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) Graham debuted her first independent concert, consisting of 18 short solos and trios that she had choreographed. This performance took place at the [48th Street Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_Street_Theatre "48th Street Theatre") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). She would later say of the concert: "Everything I did was influenced by [Denishawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn "Denishawn")."[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMansfield_Soares199256-12) On November 28, 1926, Graham and others in her company gave a dance recital at the [Klaw Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaw_Theatre "Klaw Theatre") in New York City. Around the same time she entered an extended collaboration with Japanese-American [pictorialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictorialism "Pictorialism") photographer [Soichi Sunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soichi_Sunami "Soichi Sunami").[[13]](#cite_note-13) Graham was on the faculty of [Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse_School_of_the_Theatre "Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre") when it opened in 1928.[[14]](#cite_note-peck-14)

One of Graham's students was heiress [Bethsabée de Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethsabée_de_Rothschild "Bethsabée de Rothschild") with whom she became close friends. When Rothschild moved to Israel and established the [Batsheva Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batsheva_Dance_Company "Batsheva Dance Company") in 1965, Graham became the company's first director.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

[Graham's technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique") pioneered a principle known as "contraction and release" in modern dance, which was derived from a stylized conception of breathing.[[16]](#cite_note-CraineMackrell2010-16)

In conjunction with the [1936 Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympic_Games "1936 Summer Olympic Games") in Berlin, the German government wanted to include dance in the Art Competitions that took place during the Olympics, an event that previously included architecture, sculpture, painting, music, and literature.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Although [Joseph Goebbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Goebbels "Joseph Goebbels"), Reich Minister of Propaganda, was not appreciative of the modern dance art form and changed Germany's dance from more avant-garde to traditional, he and [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") still agreed to invite Graham to represent the United States. However, the United States was not represented in the Art Competitions as Graham refused the invitation by stating:

> I would find it impossible to dance in Germany at the present time. So many artists whom I respect and admire have been persecuted, have been deprived of the right to work for ridiculous and unsatisfactory reasons, that I should consider it impossible to identify myself, by accepting the invitation, with the regime that has made such things possible. In addition, some of my concert group would not be welcomed in Germany.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004136-18)

Goebbels himself wrote her a letter assuring her that her Jewish dancers would "receive complete immunity". Graham nevertheless rejected the invitation.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004137-19)

Stimulated by the occurrences of the 1936 Olympic Games, and the propaganda that she heard through the radio from the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"), Graham created *[American Document](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Document "American Document")* in 1938. The dance expressed American ideals and democracy as Graham realized that it could empower men and inspire them to fight fascist and Nazi ideologies. American Document ended up as a patriotic statement focusing on rights and injustices of the time, representing the American people including its Native-American heritage and slavery. During the performance, excerpts from the [U.S. Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Independence_(U.S.) "Declaration of Independence (U.S.)"), Lincoln's [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), and the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") were read. These were passages that highlighted the American ideals and represented what made the American people American. For Graham, a dance needed to "reveal certain national characteristics because without these characteristics the dance would have no validity, no roots, no direct relation to life".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1938, the [Roosevelt family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_family "Roosevelt family") invited Graham to dance at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), making her the first dancer to perform there.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In the same year, [Erick Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erick_Hawkins "Erick Hawkins") became the first man to dance with her company. He officially joined her troupe the following year, dancing male lead in a number of Graham's works. They were married in July 1948 after the New York premiere of *Night Journey*.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFranko2012139-22) He left her troupe in 1951 and they divorced in 1954.

On April 1, 1958, the [Martha Graham Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Dance_Company "Martha Graham Dance Company") premiered the ballet *[Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra_(dance) "Clytemnestra (dance)")*, which would become a success.[[23]](#cite_note-23) With a score by Egyptian-born composer [Halim El-Dabh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halim_El-Dabh "Halim El-Dabh"), this ballet was a large scale work and the only full-length work in Graham's career. Graham choreographed and danced the title role, spending almost the entire duration of the performance on the stage.[[24]](#cite_note-lamothe-24) The ballet tells the story of Queen [Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra "Clytemnestra"), who is married to King [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon").
